## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Kāliṅgabodhijātaka* (Ja 479) is a narrative poem preserved in the Jātaka collection of the Pali canon [SuttaCentral]. The canonical verses recount the journey of King Kāliṅga to the Bodhi tree at Bodh Gayā, where he venerates the site of the Buddha's enlightenment with sixty thousand cartloads of flowers [Norman 1983; UNDV Conference Volume 2009]. In the course of the story, a brāhmaṇa recognizes the site as the sacred spot where previous Buddhas attained awakening by its distinct auspicious signs, such as the surrounding grasses and creepers curling clockwise (*padakkhiṇato āvattā*) [Holt et al. 2003]. As noted by K. R. Norman, the composition is thoroughly Buddhist in character and written in the archaic *āryā* metre, an indicator that the poetic stratum of the text is relatively old [Norman 1983].
While the canonical verses focus on King Kāliṅga's pilgrimage, the introductory commentarial narrative (*paccuppannavatthu*) is set at Jetavana and provides the locus classicus for early Theravāda shrine typology [SuttaCentral; Wood 2005; Bentor 1992]. In response to Anāthapiṇḍika and Ānanda seeking an object of worship for lay followers when the Buddha is absent, the text presents a threefold division of shrines (*cetiyas*): bodily relics (*sārīrika*), relics of use or association (*pāribhogika*), and commemorative or indicative shrines (*uddesika*) [Schopen 1997; Bentor 1992]. Within this framework, bodily relics are ruled out while the Buddha is alive, and an indicative image is characterized as lacking ground, thereby establishing the Bodhi tree as the legitimate *pāribhogika* surrogate for devotional veneration [Schopen 1997; Germano and Trainor 2004; DeCaroli 2015]. A slightly variant version of this narrative appears in the *Ānandabodhi* chapter of the later chronicle *Mahābodhivaṃsa* [von Hinüber 1996].
DharmaNexus identifies extensive textual overlap between the verses and the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (Catuttho bhāgo, 10 matches) [DharmaNexus]. Outside Pali, machine alignments connect the text with Kṣemendra's Tibetan *Bodhisattvāvadānakalpalatā* (D4155) and suggest low-scoring matches with the Chinese *Saṃyuktāgama* (T 99) [DharmaNexus].
